title: Some deep ocean water last touched the surface about 1,000 years ago
body: In a few places, such as the Norwegian Sea and the Weddell and Ross Seas off Antarctica, surface water becomes so cold and salty that it is dense enough to **sink to the ocean floor**. Freezing sea ice helps, because it leaves its salt behind in the water below. That sinking drives a slow, worldwide flow known as the thermohaline circulation, or the ocean's conveyor belt, a name coined by the climate scientist Wallace Broecker. The deep water creeps through the ocean basins and rises again mostly in the Indian and Pacific Oceans; the oldest of it, welling up in the North Pacific, has been on its way for about 1,000 years.

slides.prompt: Only one part of the ocean can flow all the way around the world without running into land. Where?
slides.detail: There the Antarctic Circumpolar Current links the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific Oceans, letting deep water from the Atlantic rise in the other two.

slides.heading: Why the seas off Iceland stay open
slides.text: The steady inflow of warm surface water into the far North Atlantic is what keeps the seas around Iceland and southern Greenland mostly free of sea ice all year.

slides.question: What makes surface water sink near Greenland and Antarctica?
options: Cold and salt make it dense
slides.explanation: Cold water is denser than warm water, and salty water denser than fresh. When freezing sea ice leaves extra salt behind, the surface water gets heavy enough to sink.
